Asher-Herbert Gonsiorowski, son of Julia and Moritz, was born in 1905 in Hamburg, Germany. There he completed his law studies and earned a doctorate. Asher joined a training group in Luxembourg, and with his fellow trainees he immigrated to Eretz Israel in 1936. He worked at Kfar Yedidya, studied stonecutting in Jerusalem, and finally worked as a laborer on a farm in Beit Yitzhak.

With the outbreak of the Second World War, he enlisted in the British Army and was assigned to Company 605 of the Pioneer Corps. Asher served in Egypt and in the Western Desert, at Mersa Matruh, Sollum and Tobruk. In March 1941 the corps was sent to Greece to halt the German invasion of that country. About a month later, at the end of April, the corps surrendered to the Germans, and most of its men, Asher among them, were taken prisoner. He spent about four years in German captivity. At the beginning of 1945 he was marched deep into Germany in the "Great March" of prisoners, and as a result of the hardships of the journey he died on 14 Nisan 5705 (28 March 1945). He left a sister in Eretz Israel.

His name is commemorated in the "Book of Volunteers" and in the "Journalists' Yearbook" of 5706 (1946).

Further details on his service in the British Army: Asher-Herbert Gonsiorowski (Gonsiorowski Asher (Herbert)), British service number PAL/12168, enlisted in the British Army in 1940. He was assigned to the Pioneer Corps (P.C.) in 605 Pioneer Company. His military trade was digger. His rank in the British Army was Private (Pte.). He was laid to rest in Becklingen War Cemetery, Germany, grave location 16. D. 4.
